blocks.text: Market Overview

blocks.html: Q2 2026 was another false start for US private equity: deployment, exits and fundraising weakened together. Deal value fell -37.5% QoQ to US$177.3bn, exit value nearly halved to US$102.6bn, and YTD fundraising of US$159.6bn is flowing overwhelmingly to the largest managers. Valuation marks are holding while dry powder of US$1,067bn offers only ~0.9 years of runway at the 2025 deployment pace — pressure that cuts toward deployment, not discipline. The through-line, as PitchBook puts it, is liquidity: until distributions resume in earnest, both fundraising and new deployment stay under pressure.

Deal Activity
2.1 Deal value and count

blocks.html: Deployment stalled abruptly. Q2 deal value of US$177.3bn was down 37.5% QoQ and 23.9% YoY — one of the steepest single-quarter contractions in PitchBook's dataset — while deal count held up at 2,384 (-1.1% QoQ), meaning the pullback concentrated in larger transactions. The forces were simultaneous rather than singular: a Fed that shelved cuts and debates hikes, wider direct-lending spreads, an energy-driven inflation shock, and an accelerating AI-driven reassessment of software.

blocks.text: 2.3 LBO volume in M&A context

blocks.html: PE is ceding M&A share to strategic acquirers — and the report data pack now quantifies it. Buyout/LBO value of US$734.2bn YTD represents 27.1% of the US$2,710.7bn of global M&A in H1 2026, down from 41.2% for full-year 2025 — a 14.1pp collapse to the lowest share since 2016 and the sharpest one-year drop in the series. The overall market did not shrink with it: global M&A totalled US$1,306.2bn in Q2 (up 35.3% YoY, down 18.4% from Q1's record US$1,601.2bn), and North America printed US$787.0bn across 4,476 deals (+37.4% YoY, -24.3% QoQ). Strategic buyers filled the space sponsors vacated — consistent with EY's read of US US$100m+ deal value up 88% YoY with megadeal value up 148%, and with sponsored M&A loan volume shrinking 54% QoQ while corporate borrowers more than doubled theirs.

blocks.text: 2.4 Middle market

blocks.html: The middle market (US$25m–1bn EV) held up better than the headline market — its share of all US PE buyout value rose toward ~40% as megadeals retreated (data lag one quarter, as of 31 Mar 2026). For fund selection this supports a middle-market tilt: cheaper entry, less exit-route dependence on IPOs, better recent relative performance — offset by thinner financing depth if credit tightens further.

blocks.text: 2.5 How the volume measures nest — and where private credit connects

blocks.html: The four volume measures in this report are nested cuts of one market, from broadest to narrowest: global M&A (US$2,710.7bn in H1 2026) contains both corporate-led and sponsor-led deals; North America M&A (US$1,826.5bn) is its geographic slice; US PE deal value (US$461.0bn) is the sponsor-only slice of the US market across all deal types (buyout, add-on, growth); US PE buyout/LBO (US$347.3bn) strips out growth deals; and the middle market (US$25m–1bn EV, ~US$139bn est.) is its size slice, roughly 40% of buyout value. The 'LBO volume in M&A' ratio in §2.3 (27.1%) is the top two layers divided: global buyout ÷ global M&A. Three definitional wrinkles when quoting across layers: NA includes Canada while US PE does not; US PE deal value includes growth/expansion minority deals that sit outside the M&A universe, so it is not a strict subset of the Buyout/LBO line; and every layer includes PitchBook's estimated values for undisclosed deals.

blocks.html: Private credit connects to this hierarchy on the financing side, at the third and fourth layers. Every buyout carries a debt package sourced from either the broadly syndicated loan market or private credit — and private markets financed 82% of LBOs by count as of 1Q26 — so buyout/LBO volume is the demand engine for direct-lending origination: this quarter's -37.5% QoQ fall in PE deal value is the same event as the -24% y/y decline in direct-lending origination that the Private Credit report tracks. The middle market is private credit's home turf — deals in this size band rarely access the BSL market, and the resulting loans are the collateral behind middle-market CLOs. The top two layers (global and NA M&A) sit largely outside private credit's reach: corporate-led M&A is financed with investment-grade debt and balance-sheet cash. blocks.text: 3.2 Fund performance: rolling horizon IRR

blocks.html: Rolling one-year horizon IRRs have settled in single digits, and the ordering matters as much as the level: the middle market leads at 8.7%, US PE overall runs at 7.2%, and megafunds trail at 5.7% (as of 30 Sep 2025 — performance lags ~3 quarters). The cycle context makes the reset stark: the same series peaked above 50% in the 2021 revaluation wave, swung to roughly -5% for megafunds in the 2022–23 correction, and has since flattened into a narrow single-digit band — marks have stabilised, but at a level below most funds' underwritten hurdles. In a slow-exit regime DPI is the honest measure; the distribution shortfall in §4 is precisely what keeps LP re-up capacity constrained in §5.

blocks.text: Exits & Liquidity
4.1 Exit activity

blocks.html: Distribution conditions worsened. Exit value fell to US$102.6bn (-46.3% QoQ, -7.4% YoY) on 353 exits, with US$1bn+ mega-exits anchoring more than 60% of quarterly value. The lone bright spot was the public window: listing value rose 42.2% sequentially to US$27.6bn and the count doubled to 12, though the reopening was narrow and skewed to B2B and industrials. The deals-to-exits ratio widened to 1.41 from 1.35 in 2025: the industry is still adding inventory faster than it clears it.

blocks.text: Fundraising & Dry Powder
5.1 Fundraising

blocks.html: The fundraising market is clearing only at the top. YTD capital raised of US$159.6bn across 223 funds is on pace with 2025's muted US$308.0bn, but fund counts have fallen dramatically and commitments flow overwhelmingly to the largest managers: funds under US$1bn have drawn just 16.7% of 2026 commitments, and first-time and emerging managers are squeezed hardest. The clearest growth is outside the closed-end machine — US evergreen PE assets nearly doubled over the past year to US$99bn. Median step-ups compressed to 1.44x for both buyout and all PE funds. Implication for Junson: LP-favorable terms and co-invest access are most negotiable in the sub-US$1bn cohort, where the capital shortage is acute.

blocks.text: Things We Should Know
7.1 AI is repricing PE's favourite sector

blocks.html: The AI reassessment is now a first-order PE fundamental, cutting both ways. Software slid from PE's anchor allocation to one of its least wanted — Q2 estimated software deal value of US$10.7bn, -65.7% YoY and 90.3% below peak — as AI compresses the perceived disruption timeline for incumbent software business models. The same force is rebuilding the case for the physical infrastructure that feeds it: energy YTD deal value is up 80.5%, the only major sector to grow in both count and value. For a fund allocator the test is portfolio-level: managers with heavy 2020–2022 software cohorts face both mark risk and extended holds; managers positioned in energy, industrials and AI-adjacent infrastructure get a cyclical and structural tailwind. Claim to revisit in Q3: software's share of US PE deal value stays below 15% for the rest of 2026 despite the valuation reset.

7.3 How the PE market impacts the private credit market

blocks.html: The transmission runs through three channels, all visible this quarter. Origination demand: every buyout's debt package is sourced from either the BSL market or private credit, and private markets financed 82% of LBOs by count as of 1Q26 — so the -37.5% QoQ fall in US PE deal value (§2.1) and the -24% y/y decline in direct-lending origination tracked in our Private Credit Quarterly are the same event seen from two sides. Portfolio behaviour: with sponsors in balance-sheet defense — 45% of non-refinancing BSL issuance versus a ~70% five-year average, 53% of refinancing volume, 74% of extension amendments — private credit books rotate from new deployment toward amendments, repricings and PIK toggles, which is where credit-quality signals surface first. Pricing power: scarcer new deals plus returning bank competition move the direct-lending premium around, but at 178bp over single-B BSL (2Q26, PC Quarterly §3) private credit is still being paid for illiquidity. Net: a weak PE deal tape slows private credit's growth but fattens its seasoned-book economics — the risk to watch is not volume, it is the extend-and-hope cohort inside existing books as holds lengthen (§4).

7.4 How the PE market impacts GP-stakes funds

blocks.html: A GP-stakes fund owns three cash-flow streams — management-fee earnings, carried interest, and the terminal value of the stake — and each maps to one part of this report. Fundraising (§5) drives the fee stream, the largest component of value: concentration toward large platforms is a structural tailwind for a book like GPS V's (Stonepeak, Veritas, CVC, PAI, H.I.G — ~80% of holding value), and Veritas IX's US$15.3bn close shows it; but fundraising failure is the sharpest markdown trigger in the strategy — MBK -14.2% this quarter and DivCore/Bitkraft last quarter were all fundraising-driven. Exits (§4) drive carry crystallisation, and the drought explains why only 8.2% of GPS V's US$3.4bn gross distributions are sale proceeds while 36.2% come from securitization — engineered, not market, liquidity; the offset is that longer holds extend the fee-collection period, the strategy's built-in hedge. Performance and multiples (§3) drive the marks: single-digit rolling IRRs defer carry value, and listed alt-manager prices transmit instantly — CVC's -19.2% quarter took roughly two points off GPS V's portfolio on its own. Deal activity (§2) is the slow variable, governing future carry-pool formation and successor-fund timing. Net read: fee streams are secure at scale, carry is deferred, and marks are volatile — exactly the profile GPS V prints in §9 (17th percentile on IRR, 71st on DPI).

7.5 Implications for Junson

blocks.html: Implication for Junson: treat 2026 as a selectively attractive commitment vintage — entry multiples are drifting down and competition for deals is thinner — but only with managers who can demonstrate realized DPI, not marked IRR. Maintain the pacing plan (falling multiples plus thin runway favour steady 2026–27 commitments over waiting); tilt toward middle-market buyout and energy/industrial exposure while stress-testing software-heavy GPs' 2020–22 cohorts; evaluate GP-led/continuation opportunities, where 29% of inventory held 6+ years plus below-pace GP-led volume implies unmet demand and widening LP-stake discounts. What would change our mind: quarterly exit value above US$200bn for two consecutive quarters (liquidity turning); deals-to-exits below 1.25 (inventory clearing); sub-US$1bn share of fundraising above 25% (breadth returning).

blocks.html: HPC Fund I (from Hunter Point Capital) is the only competitor with a quarterly report in hand, and the two funds' latest quarters ran in opposite directions: HPC generated +US$144m (+4.5%) of total value appreciation in 4Q25, while GPS V's GP portfolio fell -2.3% in 1Q26 — note the one-quarter timing mismatch. HPC also announced Fund II with a first close expected March 2026 — alongside GP Stakes VI's US$8.9bn, evidence that GP-stakes fundraising is clearing even in a weak PE tape.

blocks.text: 9.3 DPI benchmark: where the holdings sit on the buyout distribution curve

blocks.html: Blue Owl's own market commentary supplies the benchmark: MSCI Burgiss DPI quartile paths for the 2010, 2016, 2019 and 2021 buyout vintages (data as of 31 Dec 2025). The four cohorts are market-wide buyout-fund universes — not Blue Owl funds — chosen to show that dispersion between quartiles now exceeds dispersion between vintages, and that the 2021 cohort is depressed across all quartiles outside the top 5%. Placing the holdings on those curves at their first-investment fund ages: GPS V (age ~5, DPI 0.4x) sits at the top quartile of the 2021 cohort (0.4x at year 5) and between median (0.35x) and top quartile (0.5x) of the 2019 cohort — a solid relative DPI, with the §8 caveat that 36.2% of its gross distributions are securitization-engineered rather than exit-driven. HPC Fund I (age ~4, DPI 0.2x) sits between the median (0.15x) and top quartile (0.25x) of the 2021 cohort at year 4. The comparability caveat runs the other way, too: GP-stakes economics front-load cash (management-fee share of GP earnings) relative to buyout funds, so a same-age DPI comparison flatters GP-stakes structurally.

blocks.text: 9.4 Relative momentum and percentile trajectory

blocks.html: This is the first quarter recorded in the competitor ledger, so — as in the Private Credit report's inaugural run — the momentum exhibits show levels against the reporting-peer median rather than quarter-on-quarter change, and the trajectory charts carry a single baseline point; both become genuine time series from next quarter by appending to the ledger rather than recomputing. One momentum reading does already exist: GPS V is the only fund in the set with two net observations, and its own QoQ is negative — net blended IRR -3.1pp (10.7%→7.6%) and TVPI -0.1x (1.2x→1.1x) against 4Q25. On levels, GPS V trails the reporting-peer medians on IRR (7.6% vs 20.9%) and TVPI (1.1x vs 1.63x) but leads on DPI (0.4x vs 0.36x); its percentile ranks are 17th on IRR, 33rd on TVPI and 71st on DPI — the same shape as §9.1 and §9.3: weak on marked performance, strong on realized cash. blocks.text: 9.5 Appendix — peer universe and methodology

blocks.html: The full screen holds 33 GP-stakes and adjacent vehicles, of which 19 carry a PitchBook vintage and 7 report performance. The vintage profile shows the strategy's institutionalization: formation is sparse and episodic before 2020, then steps up to 5 funds in the 2024 vintage with ~US$9.4bn of reported aggregate size — dominated by Blue Owl GP Stakes VI's US$9.1bn — with 2025–26 vintages already forming (Trestle II, AXA IM Prime). Two reads for Junson: the competitive set for large-cap GP stakes remains effectively three platforms (Blue Owl, Petershill, and now HPC), and the entry of small first-time vehicles (US$20–640m) signals the strategy is being retailed down-market — watch for cohort-quality dilution in future vintages. Methodology: vintages follow PitchBook's first-investment convention throughout; percentile = share of reporting cohort strictly below the subject, subject excluded; manager-reported figures (GPS V, HPC) and PitchBook's lagged, self-reported figures are shown side by side but are not strictly comparable; aggregate size only sums funds that disclose it, so the size line is a floor, not a total. The cohort-dispersion (IQR) monitor from the Private Credit report is omitted: with at most two ranked funds per vintage the statistic is not meaningful; it will be reinstated on PitchBook Benchmarks buyout cohorts once that release joins the source library.
